division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

subdivision.heading: Defence to Statement of Claim, Reply to Defence and Demand for Notice

operative_text.controlling:
3.34(1)  If the defendant files a demand for notice, the demand
must be in Form 13.
(2)  The defendant must file the demand for notice and serve it on
the plaintiff within the applicable time after service of the
statement of claim on the defendant.
(3)  The applicable time is
(a) 20 days if service is effected in Alberta,
(b) one month if service is effected outside Alberta but in
Canada, and
(c) 2 months if service is effected outside Canada.
(4)  If the defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the
plaintiff, the defendant must be served with notice of any
application or proceeding in which the defendant is named as
respondent, but filing and service of the notice does not give the
defendant a right to contest liability.
(5)  If a defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the
plaintiff, the defendant may subsequently file a statement of
defence only with the Court’s permission.
(6)  Judgment or an order may be given against a defendant who
has filed and served a demand for notice only if
(a) the plaintiff applies to the Court for judgment or an order,
and
(b) notice of the application is served on the defendant.

BOOK_A.title: Demand for Notice by Defendant

BOOK_A.commentary:
England and some provinces (not Alberta) start a suit with a writ of summons requiring the defendant to file only a simple appearance document to prevent default judgment at that stage. Alberta's partial equivalent to the appearance is the demand for notice (formerly "demand of notice").It is used in Alberta only by someone who has no defence to liability, but wants notice of

later proceedings, such as an application for judgment.It prevents default judgment by the Clerk. A demand for notice does not give the right to contest liability (unless the court later allows the defendant to withdraw the demand and substitute a statement of defence ).A defendant who does not file and serve a statement of defence admits liability.The demand for notice is common where the only dispute will be about the timing and terms of the relief, especially in foreclosures.

It could be used in a damage action where the only issue is assessing the amount of damages, but defendants even in such actions often file a statement of defence. A demand for notice is a virtual invitation to the plaintiff to move for summary judgment (which is what a foreclosure order nisi/sale is). *Judgment or Order by Agreement*

BOOK_B.title: Demand for notice by defendant

commentary.text: Rule 3.34 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.34. 1. Amendment Rules Govern Withdrawal of Demand of Notice In my opinion to withdraw a Demand of Notice and replace it by a Statement of Defence is no different than the ordinary amendment of a pleading and the same rules apply. It is trite law that an amendment will be permitted where it can be made without prejudice to the opposite party or where the prejudice can be compensated with costs. When an admission has been made, as was done here by filing a Demand of Notice or where merely technical defences have been omitted and are now sought to be advanced or where there has been long delay, the court will be less likely to grant the amendment. All of the factors either for or against the exercise of the discretion to permit amendment must be weighed and that decision made which will best do justice between the parties. Canada Permanent Trust Co. v. King Art Developments Ltd. (1984), 52 A.R. 139 at 146-47 C.A. 2. Purpose of Demand of Notice Its purpose … is to give to a defendant who admits his liability under the cause of action sued on a chance to see that he is not held for more than he should be for that purpose and to present, if necessary, to the Court anything that may be helpful to it in that respect. Stone v. Vulcan Municipal Hospital District, [1930] 1 W.W.R. 839 (Alta. T.D.), per Walsh J., quoted with approval in Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), which was quoted with approval in Canada Permanent Trust Co. v. King Art Developments Ltd. (1984), 52 A.R. 139 at 146 (C.A.). 3. Effect of Demand of Notice The demand of notice results in the admission of liability by the defendant but it preserves the defendant's ability to dispute the amount sought. … where damages only were in question, by filing a demand of notice, a defendant would be entitled to have notice of a taking of account on a mortgage. Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at 378, per McDermind J., paraphrasing Canadian Mortgage Investment Co. v. Baird (1916), 10 W.W.R. 1195 (Alta. T.D.). 4. Right of Defendant The defendant is entitled to be heard on the motion required by R. 146. As Walsh J. stated in Stone v. Vulcan Municipal Hospital District, [1930] 1 W.W.R. 839 (Alta. T.D.), as quoted in Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at 379: The defendant having given its demand of notice became entitled to ‘notice of all motions against him subsequently made in the action’… The only purpose of this can be to give him an opportunity to appear upon it and his appearance would be a futile thing if he could not be heard upon the motion. This goes so far as to permit cross-examination and the calling of evidence on the issue of quantum: Lupkoski v. Lupkoski, [1974] 3 W.W.R. 377 (Alta. C.A.), at p. 381. 5. When Leave Required Master Funduk says in Alberta Treasury Branches v. Naber (1994), 161 A.R. 393 (Master), at p. 397: To deliver a statement of defence in place of a demand of notice is in essence an amendment of a pleading … Filing a statement of defence after filing a demand of notice may only occur with leave. The defendants … who initially filed demands of notice now wish to withdraw the demands of notice and to file statements of defence. It is my view that they are not entitled to do so as of right, but that leave may be granted to permit the filing of statements of defence. Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments (1983), 29 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (Q.B.), at 273, per McFadyen J. One must therefore apply for leave to replace the demand of notice with a statement of defence. The application is analogous to an application under R. 158 “to set aside a noting in default and to permit the filing of a defence. The procedure applicable thereto can be applied to this application.” See Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments (1983), 29 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 (Q.B.), at p. 277. The defendants must also show that they have a good defence on the merits. It would be entirely unproductive to permit the filing of a statement of defence in circumstances where a summary judgment application would be granted should a statement of defence be filed. Bell v. Grande Mountain Apartments, supra, at 277.

BOOK_C.title: Demand for notice by defendant
BOOK_C.operative_text_raw:
(1) If the defendant files a demand for notice, the demand must be in Form 13.
(2) The defendant must file the demand for notice and serve it on the plaintiff within the applicable time after service of the statement of claim on the defendant.
(3) The applicable time is, (a) 20 days if service is effected in Alberta, (b) one month if service is effected outside Alberta but in Canada, and (c) 2 months if service is effected outside Canada.
(4) If the defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant must be served with notice of any application or proceeding in which the defendant is named as respondent, but filing and service of the notice does not give the defendant a right to contest liability.
(5) If a defendant files a demand for notice and serves it on the plaintiff, the defendant may subsequently file a statement of defence only with the Court’s permission.
(6) Judgment or an order may be given against a defendant who has filed and served a demand for notice only if (a) the plaintiff applies to the Court for judgment or an order, and (b) notice of the application is served on the defendant.

commentary.text:
An action in which a demand for notice is filed is partially defended. Swain v. McLachlan, [2016] A.J. No. 9, 2016 ABQB 8 at para. 10 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
A defendant who files a demand for notice, in essence, admits liability on the terms alleged in the statement of claim. Richardson v. Richardson, [2018] A.J. No. 1177, 2018 ABCA 327 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.). However, a demand for notice allows the defendant to challenge the quantum of the claim. Swain v. McLachlan, [2016] A.J. No. 9, 2016 ABQB 8 at para. 10 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
A defendant who files a demand for notice cannot contest liability; however, he or she is entitled to notice of any application or proceeding in the action. Richardson v. Richardson, [2018] A.J. No. 1177, 2018 ABCA 327 at para. 8 (Alta. C.A.). Accordingly, the plaintiff A demand for notice is suited for use in rare, special circumstances. Most frequently, it is filed in response to mortgage foreclosure actions.
